\begin{hbdefinition}{def:p02-arbitrary-prop-language}{Finitary propositional language on an arbitrary set}
For an arbitrary set \(P\), \(\operatorname{Form}(P)\) is the least set
containing \(P\) and closed under the fixed finitary connectives. A valuation
is a total function \(v:P\to\{0,1\}\), extended by structural recursion. The
word ``arbitrary'' is necessary because the source completeness proof

is satisfiable iff no occurring variable \(p\) has both \(p\) and \(\neg p\)

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p02-xor-sat}{cited=Schaefer1978}{XOR-SAT tractability}
XOR satisfiability is decidable by Gaussian elimination over the two-element

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p02-two-sat}{cited=AspvallPlassTarjan1979}{2-SAT tractability}
For a 2-CNF instance without an empty clause, form the implication graph on
literals by adding directed edges from \(\overline L\) to \(K\) and from
\(\overline K\) to \(L\) for every clause \(L\lor K\), treating a unit clause
\(L\) as \(L\lor L\).  The instance
is satisfiable iff no occurring variable \(p\) has both \(p\) and \(\neg p\)
in one strongly connected component.  The test runs in \(O(N)\) time.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p12.sat.1}{thm:p12-dpll-correctness}{Correctness of the displayed DPLL logical core}
\begin{proof}
Let the current state be a residual clause set \(G\), a consistent partial
truth assignment \(u\) to variables of the original finite input \(F\), and
the unchanged finite set \(\operatorname{Var}(F)\).  Maintain both parts of the
following invariant: every original clause deleted from \(G\) already contains
a literal made true by \(u\), and every clause retained in \(G\) is exactly the
residual of its original clause after literals made false by \(u\) have been
deleted.

A unit step selects a singleton clause \(\{L\}\).  Every total satisfying
extension of \(u\) must make \(L\) true.  Extending \(u\) accordingly, deleting
clauses containing \(L\), and deleting the complement of \(L\) elsewhere
therefore preserves the invariant and preserves existence of a satisfying
extension in both directions.  At any state, including the initial state, if
\(G\) contains the empty clause, no extension of the current assignment can
satisfy that residual clause; a unit update that exposes it therefore fails.
At any state, including the initial state, if \(G\) has no clauses, each
original clause already has a true literal; an update that deletes the last
residual clause is one instance of this case.  Assigning
arbitrary truth values to the remaining original variables cannot
destroy any such witness, so the returned total assignment satisfies \(F\).

\section{First-order resolution}
\label{sec:automated-reasoning-04}

The term \emph{clause} retains its standing as a finite set of first-order
literals.  Its formula interpretation is
\(\operatorname{ucl}_{\Lang}(C)\), the universal closure of
\(\operatorname{form}_{\Lang}(C)\).  Before each inference, rename the two
parent clauses apart.  If \(A\in E\), \(\neg B\in F\), and
\(\theta_{\mathrm u}\) is a most general unifier of the atoms \(A\) and
\(B\), the active resolution rule is
\[
  \Rule[Resolution]{E\qquad F}
  {\bigl((E\setminus\set{A})\cup(F\setminus\set{\neg B})\bigr)
   \theta_{\mathrm u}}.
\]
The conclusion is the resolvent.  Factoring is also part of the active
calculus: if two same-polarity literals in \(E\) have unifiable underlying
atoms and \(\theta_{\mathrm u}\) is a most general unifier, infer
\(E\theta_{\mathrm u}\).

\begin{theorem}[Soundness of resolution]
Every structure satisfying the parent clauses of a resolution or factoring
inference satisfies its conclusion.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Renaming apart preserves the universally closed formula interpretations.
Substitution preserves satisfaction of each parent clause.  If an assignment
falsified every literal in the displayed resolvent, satisfaction of the first
substituted parent would force \(A\theta_{\mathrm u}\), while satisfaction of
the second would force \(\neg(B\theta_{\mathrm u})\).  The two atoms are
literally identical, a
contradiction.  Factoring is sound because simultaneous substitution preserves
clause satisfaction.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Refutational completeness of first-order resolution]
\label{thm:fol-resolution}
Let \(S\) be a finite equality-free set of first-order clauses.  After adding
a constant if the signature has no ground term, \(S\) is not satisfiable iff
resolution with factoring derives the empty clause.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The preceding soundness theorem proves the reverse implication.  For the
forward implication, \cref{thm:herbrand-clauses} yields a finite propositionally
unsatisfiable set of ground instances of clauses in \(S\).  Propositional
refutational completeness gives a ground resolution refutation.
\Cref{thm:resolution-lifting} replaces each ground resolution step by a first-order resolution or
factoring step whose instance is that ground step.  Induction through the
finite ground refutation yields a first-order derivation of the empty clause.
This proof depends on the two cited theorems, the existence of most general
unifiers for unifiable first-order terms, and propositional refutational
completeness; it is the
precise equality-free scope of the classical result in
\cite{Robinson1965,BachmairGanzinger2001}.  The cited complete proofs and the
step-by-step lifted derivation are not reproduced here.
\end{proof}

Bare resolution is not complete for logical equality.  One must add
an equality-complete treatment, such as equality axioms together with
resolution or a sound and complete paramodulation or superposition calculus.

\section{Practical status of unrestricted first-order search}

Under the fixed effective coding, unrestricted first-order validity is
computably enumerable but undecidable
(Theorem~\ref{thm:fol-validity-undecidable} and its immediately following
enumerability corollary;
\cite{Church1936,Turing1937}).  A sound complete proof search may therefore
run forever on an invalid input; a timeout is not a countermodel.  The statement
does not transfer without proof to every fixed signature or to the decidable
fragments catalogued in Part~2.
